> * I don't understand why the import map is being passed around so much. There's still always one import map per global, and it's easy to get to that global from any algorithm or from the "script" struct. At least one instance of this seems completely redundant, which I commented on. But e.g. why are you storing the import map in [[HostDefined]]? I realize there's probably some complexity here at the particular point in time when you're merging import maps and thus the global's import map changes, but that should be able to happen completely discretely between script parsing and execution, so I don't see why scripts should need to track individual import maps separate from the global one.

My thinking was that we need to do that in order to guarantee that once we're parsing a module tree, all modules in the tree would be resolved by the same import map. E.g. I thought it is possible that a setTimeout would inject a new import map while the a module script is being downloaded and parsed, and that new import map would start taking effect after some modules were resolved but before others.
If that's not possible for some reason, I'm happy to revert these changes.

> Given this, we should explain this in the spec, maybe around `#concept-window-import-map`. With a note that in general only the root of a loading operation will access concept-window-import-map, and otherwise it'll be threaded through.

Added



> * "resolve a module integrity metadata" seems suspicious. It should probably get an import map threaded to it?

This was indeed lacking. Should be fixed now.



> * "fetch the descendants of and link" seems suspicious. Shouldn't it be getting threaded an import map from its various callers? (per the diagram above it.)

Here I think the current state is fine, as this is being called from all the root module entry points. Therefore we don't need to thread the import map into "fetch the descendants of and link", we need it to do the threading to its descendants, which it does by setting the map on the `Record`.



> * "register an import map" has a broken assert

Indeed!!

> I'm also a bit unsure now about the cases where an import map is _not_ passed in. When is that possible? (Except workers.) We have fallbacks to the Window's import map in those cases, but I'm now questioning whether they're sound.

Let me try to enumerate the cases:
* "[fetch a single module script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-a-single-module-script)" - it's typically called by a top-level script, which is why its import map is optional (it's not being passed in these cases). The only place where it's needed as when it's called from "[fetch a single imported module script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-a-single-imported-module-script)", which is called from HostLoadImportedModule](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#hostloadimportedmodule).
* "[create a JS module script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#creating-a-javascript-module-script)" - it's called from two places: 
  - from [fetch an inline module script graph](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-an-inline-module-script-graph) which directly calls "fetch the descendants of and link", and which doesn't need import map threading (as discussed above)
  - from step 13.7 of [fetch a single module script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-a-single-module-script) which can be called from "fetch a single imported module script" and hence needs an import map threaded in.

I think that covers all of them but let me know if I missed something.

> I think I see. Because the callers all operate on URLs or inline scripts, so they didn't need to do any resolution, and so didn't need an import map. It's only for the descendants that you start doing resolution and thus start needing an import map.
> 
> This does have the slightly-strange impact that given something like

> ...

> * Make all import map arguments mandatory.

> At the same time, the current static design gives us determinism and isn’t racy. A module identifier that resolves to a certain module will continue to do so throughout the lifetime of the document. It would be good to keep that characteristic.

Has an alternative design been considered that doesn't mutate a shared global map?

For example perhaps associating maps to individual script tags?:

```html
<!-- importmap="..." would only affect the loading of this graph -->
<script type="module" src="./entry.js" importmap="./entry.importmap.json"></script>
```

This alternative design could even allow for explaining importmaps in terms of [import attributes](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-import-attributes), i.e. if you want to load a third-party module with a third-party importmap you could do:

```js
import thirdParty from "./dist/third-party.js" with { importmap: "./dist/third-party.importmap.json" }
```

I almost gave a nearly-equivlent comment yesterday but was afraid I was misunderstanding something. So I'm glad you spoke up @Jamesernator.

My draft example was literally:

```js
await import("./dist/third-party.js", { withMap: "./dist/third-party.importmap.json"})
import thirdParty from "./dist/third-party.js" withMap "./dist/third-party.importmap.json"
```

## Concerns with mutating a shared global map

1. I don't see any discussion about risks, possible adverse side effects, or security. 

Consider a dynamic ``const bcrypt = await import("/path/to/bcrypt.js")`` written by a site author. Right now they have full confidence that the import will either load what they expect or throw an error. I'm not convinced that letting browser extensions break that assumption won't lead to new attack vectors. While I believe browser extensions can already affect the top level import map, its still not clear to me that dynamic changes are not more risky.

2. I don't see discussion about adverse side effects.

As I understand it, the proposal has side effects due to this being a global map. E.g. loading a brower extension can change the import behavior of non-browser-extension imports. Extensions often **do not** want side effects: case-in-point the motivating usecase at the top ([this one](https://github.com/WICG/import-maps/issues/248)) does not want side effects, it just wants to map-imports for extension1, not for extension2.

If extension1 global-mutates import-map for A
If extension2 global-mutates import-map for A

IMO extension-loading order creates a unnecessary race condition where extension1 overrides extnesion2's import map, along with extension2's developer having no good way to debug when-and-why their extension broke. (And even once they do figure out why there is basically no solution since telling the user to change the load order is impractical, they have to go back to square1 of bundling everything to be reliable)

> Has an alternative design been considered that doesn't mutate a shared global map?

That would significantly part from the current design of import maps, and would introduce potentially significant delays as each script would have to wait for its own map.

> and would introduce potentially significant delays as each script would have to wait for its own map.

This is effectively true anyway as the document loading will be blocked by the (potentially large) inline import maps. Browsers could easily fetch associated import maps in parallel with the script (along with preload links, which most people should be using for dependent imports *anyway*).

A couple of points to address pointed out by @hiroshige-g elsewhere:
* in "Already-resolved specifier and multiple rules redefining it", we should drop all the relevant rules and not just the most specific one.
* In the "merge existing and new import maps" algorithm, in "For each pair of resolvedSetCopy, remove newImportMapImports[pair's specifier]", we should also remove any of the specifier's prefixes, as they also can be used for resolution.

Given https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10528#issuecomment-2333366841 is addressed, I feel the #top-level-resolved-module-set and #scoped-resolved-module-map mechanism working correctly/consistently (at least not breaking invariants in the spec and impl) for avoiding changing existing resolution results.

Now I'm wondering if we can simplify the mechanism. Instead of #scoped-resolved-module-map, how about:

- Record the set of (baseURL, specifier) pairs at [#resolve-a-module-specifier](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#resolve-a-module-specifier) (instead of #top-level-resolved-module-set and #scoped-resolved-module-map)
- Introduce #merge-existing-and-new-import-maps, a matching procedure similar to Step 6-13 of the original https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#resolve-a-module-specifier, but instead of resolving specifiers using the first matching rules, remove all the matching rules from newImportMap (see the attached doc below for concrete details)
In #merge-existing-and-new-import-maps, for each of the recorded (baseURL, specifier), call #remove conflicting rules from import map given baseURL, specifier, and newImportMap.

By doing so,

- We can deduplicate separate logic for resolution and merging: instead of determining if new rules are conflicting with existing resolutions using #scoped-resolved-module-map, we can go through the same matching logic for resolution and conflict checking. This simplifies the logic as well as debugging/mental model by users.
- We can avoid deep copies of the import maps and multiple entries added to scoped-resolved-module-map per specifier resolution (i.e. multiplied by the number of '/'s in base URLs), etc. (I feel this can be faster but I haven't investigated thoroughly e.g. its computational complexity though.)
- The behavior is the same (I feel so, but please double check -- I also double check later).

I put more concrete spec sketch at
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1le5_AUH4H_t3FoGMLctaSh2opJy4_fLskkYhfhnikAI/edit#bookmark=id.szh1i7w4nf27

Also I came up with some examples/cases that might be worth clarifying:

Mentioning that a rule in the newly added import maps are removed in two ways is helpful:

- Rule 1: if the existing import map has a rule with exactly the same specifier and scope (if any).
- Rule 2: if the new rule can potentially affect the resolution of an already resolved specifier

And some clarifying examples:
- Rule 1: "conflicting rules" are exact matching only.
- Rule 2: new rules are removed if they **_potentially_** affect the existing resolution, even if they **_actually_** don't. (not so sure how to explain though)

I put complete examples to https://docs.google.com/document/d/1le5_AUH4H_t3FoGMLctaSh2opJy4_fLskkYhfhnikAI/edit#bookmark=id.9g3ligs9j9yh

I've done a high level review of this proposal and while I'm generally in favour I have a concern about the merging of import maps.

The current approach seems to be to ignore conflicts between import maps with earlier rules taking precedence and with no indication that this has happened.

This results in the situation where we can load the wrong URL (from a previous, perhaps injected, import map) despite the page explicitly specifying the URL that should be used. This seems wrong.

The most cautious approach here would be to flag conflicting rules when merging import maps and then throw if an attempt is made to resolve a specifier which has conflicts. Another possibility would be to fire an error when a conflict is detected.

What do you think?

Er, thanks for the context, that clarifies the intention.

Then, how about separate the spec and the specific efficient algorithm for implementing the spec?
For example, in the spec we write:

- A global object has a `resolved module set`, a set of (string, string) pairs, initially empty.
- Append (`base URL`, `specifier`) to `resolved module set`, on specifier resolution.
- To `check conflict` (name TBD) given (`scope`, `specifierKey`) in the new import map: return true if there is any (`base URL`, `specifier`) in `resolved module set` such that `scope` is a prefix of `base URL` and `specifierKey` is a prefix of `specifier`. (just sketching; I might have to add more import-map-specific conditions here)
- On import map merging, for each `scope` and (`specifierKey`, `value`) rules, remove the rul if `check conflict` given `scope` and `specifierKey` returns true (`scope` = empty string for the top-level rules).

And add a note that we can/should implement `check conflict` efficiently using efficient data structure for  `resolved module set` and/or efficient algorithms for  `check conflict` (like `O(log n)` where `n` is the size of `resolved module set`).

This is to:
Not to miss the intention and the corner cases deep in the optimized algorithms.
Allow implementers to optimize their implementation more easily, as there can be implementation/optimization choices other than using #scoped-resolved-module-map.

More on complexity analysis: So for

- `n` = the number of specifier resolution
- `m` = the number of rules in the added import map,
- `b` = the average number of slashes (`/`s) in a base URL,
- `s` = the average number of slashes (`/`s) in a specifier,

and our intention is to avoid `O(n)` at the time of import map merging.

The current PR is roughly

- `O(bsn log n)` recording time in total in specifier resolution (`O(n)` resolution * `O(b)` scope/base URL prefixes * `O(s)` specifier prefixes) for recording #scoped-resolved-module-map etc.
- `O(m log n)` per added import map, checking each rule in `O(log n)` time.

assuming the prefixes are managed by spans without copying underlying original strings (which isn't/can't be done on the spec text though?).

I feel (not concretely thinking though) we can further optimize the algorithm to `O(n log n)` recording time and `O(m log n)` per added import map (but for now I'm just exploring the space and am not intending to actually optimize the algorithm on the spec/impl right now).

> My thinking was that we need to do that in order to guarantee that once we're parsing a module tree, all modules in the tree would be resolved by the same import map. E.g. I thought it is possible that a setTimeout would inject a new import map while the a module script is being downloaded and parsed, and that new import map would start taking effect after some modules were resolved but before others. If that's not possible for some reason, I'm happy to revert these changes.

As a general rule, I don't feel any per-module-tree separation wouldn't work (at least completely) because the submodules of multiple module trees are mixed and a specific submodule can be loaded in the context of any of the referencing module trees.
So I'm dubious the per-module-tree import maps copying in the current PR would work, as well as other attempts to specifying per-module-tree import maps e.g. in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10528#issuecomment-2280200240 https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10528#issuecomment-2282190967

(*) It's still possible to create per-module-tree separation (e,g, allowing incomplete separation in some cases), but probably needs more thoughts on in which case the separation must work and in which case incomplete separation is allowed. (Or should we think about more per-module-tree-separated module loading, which largely revamps the module loading? This has been discussed in many contexts but didn't actually happen)

And specific issues below.
For example, we have:

```
<script type="importmap">(empty import map)</script>
<script src="root1.js" type="module"></script>
<script type="importmap">{"imports": {"./app.js": "./app2.js"}}</script>
<script src="root2.js" type="module"></script>

root1.js: import "./app.js"; import "./sub.js";
sub.js: import "./app.js";
root2.js: import "./app.js"; import "./sub.js";
```

And the intention of the copying import maps per-module-tree is to make `./app.js` in root1.js and sub.js loaded from root1.js to be resolved using the initial import map (in this case, empty import map) to `./app.js`, not to `./app2.js`, regardless of whether `root1.js` is loaded before or after the import map update.

If root1.js is loaded before the import map update, then the only rule of the updated import map `"./app.js": "./app2.js"` is rejected, so all specifiers are resolved using an empty import map.

Otherwise (if root1.js is loaded after the import map update):

- `./app.js` in root1.js is resolved to `app.js` using the copied import map.
- `./app.js` in root2.js is resolved to `app2.js` using the updated import map.
- `./app.js` in sub.js is resolved either to `app.js` or  `app2.js`, depending on e.g. which of root1.js/root2.js is loaded first.

And this is

- (1) Incomplete separation: the per-module-tree separation is anyway incomplete: multiple `./app.js` specifiers in a same module tree (either root1.js or root2.js) can be mapped differently.
- (2) breaking invariants. The invariant of "specifier resolution result (given the same base URL and specifier) can't be changed" is broken. We check that the updated import map doesn't change the existing specifier resolutions, but after the check passes, we resolve `./app.js` using old/new import maps, leading different resolution results.
- (3) maybe it's harder to infer which version of import maps is used for `./sub.js`. If we always use the global import map, then the import map for `./sub.js` only depends on the timing of `./sub.js` loading (whether before or after the import map update). With copied import maps, we have to go deeper into the module loading (e.g. depending on which of root1.js/root2.js is loaded first), which can be harder to reason or even unexposed for users.

My preference is (like other non-import-map-related per-module-tree separation) to abandon the per-module-tree separation and always use the global import maps.

I was more permissive for (1) incomplete separation if it's still useful for developers (not sure actually it is though), but I found (2) broken invariants today. We might be able to fix the invariants e.g. by updating it to "specifier resolution result (given the same base URL and specifier **and import map**) can't be changed", but I doubt it worth doing given the incompleteness of separation as well as added complexity (probably we should go through the discussion like (*) above).

> * `O(bsn log n)` recording time in total in specifier resolution (`O(n)` resolution * `O(b)` scope/base URL prefixes * `O(s)` specifier prefixes) for recording #scoped-resolved-module-map etc.

Where is the `n log n` part coming from?
IMO, the current complexity is `O(b + s)` (for each one of the `n` resolutions), as all the relevant set/map operations can be done in `O(1)`


> * `O(m log n)` per added import map, checking each rule in `O(log n)` time.

`log n` part: just because I basically tend to use `O(log n)` (tree-based data structure such as `std::map`) for map/set operations to limit the upper bound/worst-case estimate, instead of `O(1)`, but I don't feel this is a big difference (and the current PR doesn't assume any underlying implementation of map/set).

`n` part: I just multiply by `n` to get the total time for all `n` resolutions. Still it's `O(bs log n)` or `O(bs)` per resolution, depending on per-map/set operation complexity.

`b + s` or `bs` part: The current PR itself is `O(b + s)` per resolution, while I was assuming https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10528/files#r1755220941 that leads `O(bs)` per resolution.

https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10528#issuecomment-2342416828

The behavior without copying the import maps per-module-tree:

If root1.js is loaded before the import map update, then the only rule of the updated import map `"./app.js": "./app2.js"` is rejected, so all specifiers are resolved using an empty import map (the same as above).

Otherwise,

- `./app.js` in root1.js is resolved to `app2.js` using the updated import map.
- `./app.js` in root2.js is resolved to `app2.js` using the updated import map.
- `./app.js` in sub.js is resolved either to `app2.js`.

So more like `./app.js` specifiers resolution results are all `app.js` or all `app2.js` (not the mixture of the two), depending on loading timing.

In summary,

`./app.js` in `root1.js`, `root2.js`, `sub.js` are resolved to:
- With per-module-tree copying: either of:
    - `app.js`, `app.js`, `app.js`
    - `app.js`, `app2.js`, `app.js`
    - `app.js`, `app2.js`, `app2.js`
- Without per-module-tree copying: either of:
    - `app.js`, `app.js`, `app.js`
    - `app2.js`, `app2.js`, `app2.js`

> `log n` part: just because I basically tend to use `O(log n)` (tree-based data structure such as `std::map`) for map/set operations to limit the upper bound/worst-case estimate, instead of `O(1)`, but I don't feel this is a big difference (and the current PR doesn't assume any underlying implementation of map/set).
> 
> `n` part: I just multiply by `n` to get the total time for all `n` resolutions. Still it's `O(bs log n)` or `O(bs)` per resolution, depending on per-map/set operation complexity.
> 
> `b + s` or `bs` part: The current PR itself is `O(b + s)` per resolution, while I was assuming https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10528/files#r1755220941 that leads `O(bs)` per resolution.

> The behavior without copying the import maps per-module-tree:
> 
> If root1.js is loaded before the import map update, then the only rule of the updated import map `"./app.js": "./app2.js"` is rejected, so all specifiers are resolved using an empty import map (the same as above).
> 
> Otherwise,
> 
> * `./app.js` in root1.js is resolved to `app2.js` using the updated import map.
> * `./app.js` in root2.js is resolved to `app2.js` using the updated import map.
> * `./app.js` in sub.js is resolved either to `app2.js`.
> 
> So more like `./app.js` specifiers resolution results are all `app.js` or all `app2.js` (not the mixture of the two), depending on loading timing.
> 
> In summary,
> 
> `./app.js` in `root1.js`, `root2.js`, `sub.js` are resolved to:
> 
> * With per-module-tree copying: either of:
>   
>   * `app.js`, `app.js`, `app.js`
>   * `app.js`, `app2.js`, `app.js`
>   * `app.js`, `app2.js`, `app2.js`
> * Without per-module-tree copying: either of:
>   
>   * `app.js`, `app.js`, `app.js`
>   * `app2.js`, `app2.js`, `app2.js`

Note that while it may be stating the obvious, it could be worth noting that warnings can be skipped when the values are equal for all merge operations,

One thing that's still worrying me a little is the size of the data being stored here. Consider an application with 1000 modules, where each of those modules have 5 imports, that's 5000 entries in this map. Since most imports are relative URLs and not bare specifiers, we are storing the specifier, baseURL and resolved URL across all 5000 entries. At 50 bytes a URL, two URLs, and 20 bytes per specifier, that might be around 600KiB for just a simple app. Of course there's probably lots of smart ways to optimize this, baseURLs being hierarchical, adding some extra string sharing etc.

I'm not saying it should be done necessarily, but there's one design tradeoff that could be made that might help reduce the data size by more than 50%, that could be worth discussing, and that's to not permit URL remapping for any full URL maps once that URL or URL prefix has been imported, regardless of scope shadowing.

This way, instead of storing every single specifier in the resolved module set, we can having two smaller sets: (1) the resolved URL set, and (2) the bare specifier resolved module set. This is based on the observation that relative specifiers are usually at least as common as bare specifiers, and often more so. We then don't need to store `asURL` on resolved module records, and can instead have a single optimized data structure tracking bare specifiers across their parent URL usage.

For that same 1000 module app, with 5 imports per module, maybe 2500 of the import specifiers were relative or URL imports and 2500 of the import specifiers were bare specifiers. We now store only 1000 entries in the imported URL set, and 2500 in the bare specifier module set as just parent + bare specifier, resulting in of the order of 50KiB + 175KiB = 225KiB at less than 40% of the size. If the relative / full URL count is higher that also improves.

The utility of URL remapping may not be lost if we don't support scoped remapping of URLs that have already been imported in dynamic import maps workflows, so that this might not be such a hard tradeoff to make. In many cases, the URLs being remapped in these workflows are local to the scope anyway and part of the private contracts of the package where the URL being mapped wouldn't have been otherwise imported, so wanting to support this may go against concepts of package and scope isolation anyway.

Would be interested to hear thoughts further.
